name: Insulin lispro
className: Rapid-acting insulin analogue; also premixed with insulin lispro protamine (biphasic)

formulations.label: Solution 100 units/mL, rapid-acting (vial, cartridge, pre-filled pen)
formulations.note: Pre-filled pens and cartridges are for subcutaneous use only; the vial can also be given intravenously. A separate 200 units/mL pen exists (separate SmPC, not covered here): units shown in the dose window need no conversion between strengths.

src.q: Each ml contains 100 units of insulin lispro* (equivalent to 3.5mg).
The KwikPen, Junior KwikPen and Tempo Pen are only suitable for subcutaneous injections.
no dose conversion should be done when transferring a patient to a new strength or to a pen with a different dose step

formulations.label: Biphasic suspension 50/50 (insulin lispro 50% / insulin lispro protamine 50%), 100 units/mL
formulations.note: Premixed rapid + intermediate-acting insulin. Subcutaneous only; never intravenous.

src.q: consists of 50% insulin lispro solution and 50% insulin lispro protamine suspension
Under no circumstances should Humalog Mix50 be given intravenously.

formulations.label: Biphasic suspension 25/75 (insulin lispro 25% / insulin lispro protamine 75%), 100 units/mL
formulations.note: Premixed rapid + intermediate-acting insulin (the clinic lists it as 75/25). Subcutaneous only; never intravenous.

src.q: consists of 25% insulin lispro solution and 75% insulin lispro protamine suspension
Under no circumstances should Humalog Mix25 be given intravenously.

brandPrescribing.t: Prescribe insulin by brand name (SPS, citing NICE guidance), and make sure the patient gets a device they have been trained to use. Where one brand comes in more than one strength or device, the brand name alone is not enough: also state the strength and device (SPS).

src.q: NICE guidance recommends insulins are prescribed by brand name.
It is important to ensure patients receive an administration device they have been trained to use.
Where a single insulin brand is available in multiple strengths or delivery devices, using only a brand name is insufficient.

items.t: Dose is individual, set by the physician to the patient's needs. Give shortly before meals (onset about 15 minutes; can be given within 0 to 15 minutes of a meal) or, when necessary, soon after meals. Duration 2 to 5 hours. Can be used with a longer-acting insulin or oral sulfonylurea on medical advice.

src.q: The dose should be determined by the physician, according to the requirement of the patient.
Humalog may be given shortly before meals. When necessary Humalog can be given soon after meals.
Insulin lispro has a rapid onset of action (approximately 15 minutes), thus allowing it to be given closer to a meal (within zero to 15 minutes of the meal)
Humalog can be used in conjunction with a longer-acting insulin or oral sulphonylurea agents, on the advice of a physician.

items.t: Basal + mealtime regimens: patients on a basal insulin must optimise the doses of both insulins to control glucose across the whole day, particularly fasting/nocturnal glucose.

src.q: any patient also on basal insulin must optimise dosage of both insulins to obtain glucose control across the whole day, particularly nocturnal/fasting glucose control

items.t: Dose is individual, set by the physician. Give shortly before meals, or soon after meals when necessary. The protamine component acts like a basal (NPH) insulin.

src.q: The dosage should be determined by the physician, according to the requirement of the patient. Humalog Mix50 may be given shortly before meals.
The dosage should be determined by the physician, according to the requirement of the patient. Humalog Mix25 may be given shortly before meals.
The duration of action of the insulin lispro protamine suspension component of Humalog Mix50 is similar to that of a basal insulin (NPH).

items.t: Hypoglycaemia warning symptoms may be different or less pronounced with long-standing diabetes, intensified insulin therapy, diabetic neuropathy or medicines such as beta-blockers. Uncorrected hypo- or hyperglycaemia can cause loss of consciousness, coma or death.

src.q: Conditions which may make the early warning symptoms of hypoglycaemia different or less pronounced include long duration of diabetes, intensified insulin therapy, diabetic nerve disease or medications such as beta-blockers.
Uncorrected hypoglycaemic or hyperglycaemic reactions can cause loss of consciousness, coma, or death.

items.t: Inadequate doses or stopping treatment, especially in insulin-dependent patients, can cause hyperglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis (potentially lethal).

src.q: may lead to hyperglycaemia and diabetic ketoacidosis; conditions which are potentially lethal

items.t: Rapid-acting analogue: if hypoglycaemia occurs, it may come earlier after injection than with soluble human insulin.

src.q: if hypoglycaemia occurs, it may occur earlier after an injection when compared with soluble human insulin

items.t: Insulin requirement may rise with illness or emotional upset; dose changes may be needed with more exercise or a change in diet. Exercise straight after a meal may increase hypoglycaemia risk.

src.q: Insulin requirements may be increased during illness or emotional disturbances.
Exercise taken immediately after a meal may increase the risk of hypoglycaemia.

items.t: Rotate injection sites (lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis delay absorption and worsen control). A sudden move to an unaffected site has caused hypoglycaemia: monitor blood glucose after a site change; antidiabetic doses may need adjusting.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to perform continuous rotation of the injection site to reduce the risk of developing lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis.
A sudden change in the injection site to an unaffected area has been reported to result in hypoglycaemia.

items.t: With pioglitazone: heart failure has been reported (especially with risk factors). Watch for heart failure, weight gain and oedema; stop pioglitazone if cardiac symptoms worsen.

src.q: patients should be observed for signs and symptoms of heart failure, weight gain and oedema. Pioglitazone should be discontinued, if any deterioration in cardiac symptoms occurs.

items.t: Medication errors: patients must check the insulin label before every injection (two pen strengths and other insulins exist) and must be able to read the dose counter; blind or poorly sighted patients need help from a trained person.

src.q: Patients must be instructed to always check the insulin label before each injection to avoid accidental mix-ups between the two different strengths of Humalog KwikPen as well as other insulin products.
Patients who are blind or have poor vision must be instructed to always get help/assistance from another person who has good vision and is trained in using the insulin device.

items.t: One connected pre-filled pen contains a magnet that may interfere with implanted electronic devices such as pacemakers (field about 1.5 cm).

items.t: Lower the insulin requirement (hypoglycaemia risk): oral hypoglycaemics, salicylates (e.g. aspirin), sulfonamide antibiotics, MAOIs, SSRIs, some ACE inhibitors (captopril, enalapril), angiotensin II receptor blockers, beta-blockers, octreotide, alcohol. The SmPC says the physician should be consulted when other medicines are used.

src.q: Insulin requirements may be reduced in the presence of medicinal products with hypoglycaemic activity, such as oral hypoglycaemics, salicylates (for example, acetylsalicylic acid), sulpha antibiotics

items.t: Raise the insulin requirement: oral contraceptives, corticosteroids, thyroid replacement therapy, danazol, beta2 stimulants (e.g. salbutamol, terbutaline).

items.t: GLP-1 receptor agonists (MHRA): when one is added to insulin, an insulin dose reduction may be considered to lower hypoglycaemia risk, but reduce insulin stepwise with blood glucose self-monitoring; abrupt reduction or stopping of insulin has led to diabetic ketoacidosis. GLP-1 receptor agonists are not substitutes for insulin.

src.q: blood glucose self-monitoring is necessary when adjusting the dose of insulin, particularly when GLP-1 receptor agonist therapy is initiated and insulin is reduced
Abrupt discontinuation or reduction in insulin doses can lead to poor glycaemic control, with a risk of diabetic ketoacidosis.

items.t: Data from a large number of pregnancies show no adverse effect of insulin lispro on pregnancy or the fetus/newborn. Keep good glucose control throughout; requirements usually fall in the first trimester and rise in the second and third. Careful monitoring of glucose control and general health is essential.

src.q: Data on a large number of exposed pregnancies do not indicate any adverse effect of insulin lispro on pregnancy or on the health of the foetus/newborn.
Insulin requirements usually fall during the first trimester and increase during the second and third trimesters.
Careful monitoring of glucose control, as well as general health, is essential in pregnant patients with diabetes.

items.t: UKTIS/BUMPS: insulin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes; there are no known risks to the baby. Insulin around delivery can cause short-lived low blood glucose in the newborn, which is checked after birth.

src.q: Insulin can be used in pregnancy to treat diabetes.
There are no known risks to your baby from using insulin in pregnancy.
Insulin use around the time of delivery can lead to your baby having low blood sugar for a short period after birth.

items.t: Breastfeeding women may need changes in insulin dose, diet or both.

items.t: SPS: any insulin can be used during breastfeeding (insulin is a preferred choice); as a precaution, monitor the infant for signs of hypoglycaemia (drowsiness, pallor, sweating or shakiness) and for adequate weight gain.

src.q: Any insulin can be used during breastfeeding, although monitoring is still recommended.
As a precaution, monitor the infant for signs of hypoglycaemia, including drowsiness, appearing pale, or being sweaty or shaky. Monitor for adequate weight gain.

items.t: No impairment of fertility in animal studies.

src.q: Insulin lispro did not induce fertility impairment in animal studies

items.t: Hypoglycaemia: the most frequent adverse effect (no frequency given; depends on dose, diet and exercise).

src.q: Hypoglycaemia is the most frequent undesirable effect of insulin therapy

items.t: Local injection-site allergy (redness, swelling, itching) is common; usually settles in days to weeks.

src.q: Local allergy in patients is common. Redness, swelling, and itching can occur at the site of insulin injection.

items.t: Lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis at injection sites (delay absorption).

src.q: Lipodystrophy and cutaneous amyloidosis may occur at the injection site and delay local insulin absorption.

items.t: Oedema, particularly when poor control is quickly improved by intensified therapy.

src.q: Cases of oedema have been reported with insulin therapy, particularly if previous poor metabolic control is improved by intensified insulin therapy.

items.t: Severe hypoglycaemia can cause loss of consciousness and, in extreme cases, death. Mild: oral glucose or sugar. Moderately severe: glucagon IM/SC, then oral carbohydrate. No response to glucagon (or glucagon unavailable): IV glucose. Give a meal on recovery and keep observing, as hypoglycaemia may recur.

src.q: Severe hypoglycaemia may lead to loss of consciousness, and in extreme cases, death.
Correction of moderately severe hypoglycaemia can be accomplished by intramuscular or subcutaneous administration of glucagon, followed by oral carbohydrate when the patient recovers sufficiently.
Patients who fail to respond to glucagon must be given glucose solution intravenously.
Sustained carbohydrate intake and observation may be necessary because hypoglycaemia may recur after apparent clinical recovery.

items.t: Systemic (generalised) allergy is rare but may be life-threatening: widespread rash, shortness of breath, wheezing, low blood pressure, fast pulse, sweating.

src.q: Systemic allergy, which is rare but potentially more serious, is a generalised allergy to insulin.
Severe cases of generalised allergy may be life-threatening.

src.q: The use of dosages which are inadequate or discontinuation of treatment

items.t: Pump use: a pump malfunction or blocked infusion set can cause a rapid rise in glucose; stop the infusion during a hypoglycaemic episode until resolved.

src.q: A pump malfunction or obstruction of the infusion set can result in a rapid rise in glucose levels.
In the event of a hypoglycaemic episode, the infusion should be stopped until the episode is resolved.

items.t: Blood glucose after any change of injection site.

items.t: Intravenous use: frequent blood glucose monitoring is required.

src.q: Frequent monitoring of the blood glucose levels is required.

items.t: MHRA (high-strength, combination and biosimilar insulins): monitor glucose closely after starting a new insulin product and in the following weeks; doses and timing of other insulins and antidiabetic treatment may need adjusting.

items.t: Pump: consider reducing or stopping the infusion if low blood glucose is repeated or severe.

src.q: If repeated or severe low blood glucose levels occur consider the need to reduce or stop an insulin infusion.

items.t: Subcutaneous injection into upper arm, thigh, buttock or abdomen; rotate sites so the same site is used no more than about once a month. Avoid entering a blood vessel; do not massage the site.

src.q: Subcutaneous administration should be in the upper arms, thighs, buttocks, or abdomen.

items.t: Vial only: may be given intravenously (e.g. ketoacidosis, acute illness, peri-operative), as a bolus or infusion of 0.1 to 1.0 units/mL in sodium chloride 0.9% or glucose 5% (stable 48 hours at room temperature). Pump use: compatible pumps only; do not mix with other insulin in a pump.

src.q: If necessary, Humalog may also be administered intravenously, for example: for the control of blood glucose levels during ketoacidosis, acute illnesses or during intra and post operative periods.
Infusion systems at concentrations from 0.1 units/ml to 1.0 units/ml insulin lispro in 0.9% sodium chloride or 5% dextrose are stable at room temperature for 48 hours.
When used with an insulin infusion pump, Humalog should not be mixed with any other insulin.

items.t: Mixing in a syringe with a longer-acting insulin (vial): draw up the rapid-acting insulin first; mixing only on medical advice.
